regions.power_system: Six interconnected utilities (Golden Valley Electric Association/GVEA, Chugach Electric, Matanuska Electric, Homer Electric, Anchorage's municipal successor, and the City of Seward) share the Railbelt grid from Fairbanks to the Kenai Peninsula. GVEA generated more than 80% of its power from fossil fuels (coal, diesel and naphtha) as of May 2025 reporting. Its largest customer, the Fort Knox gold mine, draws about 16% of GVEA's total output; Northern Star's Pogo mine draws a grid load its own 2025 corporate report labels 'Pogo GRID 16 MW'.
regions.price: Governor Dunleavy's stated (unmet) Railbelt target is 10 cents/kWh; GVEA burns roughly 200,000 tons of Usibelli coal a year under a contract signed in August [2024]

regions.nuclear_position: No state ban. SB 177 (2022) and DEC's 18 AAC 87 siting regulation (effective 2023) already permit microreactor siting statewide, Railbelt included (see alaska-legal-framework). No Railbelt utility has itself taken a formal board position for or against a reactor.
regions.microreactor_activity: May 2026: the Alaska Center for Energy and Power organized a tour of Idaho National Laboratory for utility executives including staff from Golden Valley Electric Association, to view Radiant's Kaleidos microreactor test facility and Oklo's 75 MW Aurora construction site. ACEP's own account of the trip raises, as an open question rather than a utility commitment, whether Oklo's 5 MW Eielson microreactor could be followed by 'a larger 75 MW reactor at the same location supplying power to the GVEA's grid.' No RFI, site-permit application, or GVEA board vote on nuclear was found.
blockers: No Railbelt utility has issued an RFI or committed capital to a reactor study
A Cook Inlet natural gas shortage and a federal freeze on GVEA's roughly $500 million renewables funding package (as of May 2025) are consuming utility bandwidth ahead of any nuclear decision
GVEA reversed a 2022 board vote to close a coal plant and instead signed a new Usibelli coal-supply contract
regions.microreactor_read: The Railbelt's own energy establishment (ACEP) is already treating a reactor at Eielson-scale-and-up as a live conversation because Fort Knox and Pogo prove 16 MW+ industrial loads exist on this grid; the missing piece is a utility RFI or site permit, not the enabling law, which has existed since 2023.

regions.power_system: Alaska Village Electric Cooperative (AVEC) alone serves 59 locations across rural Alaska, each village an isolated microgrid with no interconnection to the next; Nome, Kotzebue, Bethel and Utqiagvik each have their own separate municipal or cooperative diesel utility outside AVEC. AVEC adjusts customer bills every few months through an RCA-approved Cost of Power Adjustment (COPA) filing layered on top of a base Energy Charge.

regions.nuclear_position: No PCE-community utility has taken a position on nuclear power. State law (SB 177, 2022) and DEC's siting regulation (18 AAC 87, effective 2023) apply statewide and are not community-specific.
regions.microreactor_activity: None found at any individual PCE community. Searched AVEC's own news posts and RCA filing notices; found only diesel/COPA rate mechanics and PCE-funding advocacy testimony to the legislature, no reactor studies.
blockers: Most individual PCE villages draw well under 1 MW, far below any current microreactor's minimum output
58 separate diesel microgrids mean a reactor would have to be sited at a hub community and would still leave most villages on diesel
AVEC posted an operating loss in 2025 by its own reporting, leaving no obvious capital sponsor for new generation
regions.microreactor_read: Rural PCE villages carry the sector's best-regulated diesel price signal (a published base rate plus a disclosed fuel-surcharge mechanism) but the worst-matched load; a reactor needs a hub-and-aggregation buyer like the tribal utility in the tanana-chiefs prospect, not any single PCE village.

regions.power_system: Alaska's large mines split between grid-tied and diesel-only. Kensington (Coeur Alaska, underground gold, Lynn Canal) runs entirely on-site diesel: 'annual fuel consumption expected to be around 3 million gallons at full production.' Greens Creek (Hecla, Admiralty Island) has purchased surplus hydropower from Alaska Electric Light & Power since 2006, and 'since 2009, hydropower has provided 77% of Greens Creek's energy needs,' though in 2025 low precipitation cut that back and '62% of the mine's electricity [was] purchased from the grid' (i.e. thermal-backed). Fort Knox and Pogo are grid-tied to the Railbelt (see alaska-railbelt-utilities). Donlin Gold (not yet built) would need its own dual-fuel power plant, fed by a 315-mile gas pipeline. Graphite One's Graphite Creek project forecasts a 12.5 MW draw, twice Nome's own load.

regions.microreactor_activity: Graphite One's own SVP of Operations named nuclear power as an option for the Graphite Creek mine in April 2025 reporting: 'The nuclear is very favorable because it's got no carbon footprint, but they're not far enough along yet, and they've got to be socially acceptable.' This is the clearest on-record civilian-mine interest in nuclear power in Alaska outside Red Dog. No site study, RFI or vendor engagement was found beyond that statement.

regions.microreactor_read: Graphite One is the cleanest small-mine microreactor lead in Alaska after Red Dog: a company executive has already put nuclear on the list of options at a forecast 12.5 MW load, conditioned only on vendor maturity and social acceptability, not on cost or law.

regions.power_system: Not a utility record; covers the state-level rules that apply to every Alaska record above. Alaska Statute 18.45 (as amended by SB 177, 2022, defining a microreactor as no more than 50 MW) and its implementing regulation 18 AAC 87 govern microreactor siting permits statewide.
regions.nuclear_position: SB 177, signed by Governor Dunleavy in 2022, defines a microreactor as an advanced reactor of no more than 50 MW and removes the prior requirement that the legislature designate land before DEC can issue a siting permit (legislative designation is still required only for sites in an unorganized borough). DEC's implementing regulation, 18 AAC 87 (Nuclear Facility Siting), took effect August 23, 2023, and DEC's own regulation tracker shows it 'up to date' with no amendment since, through 2025-2026: applicants need a DEC siting permit plus municipal/borough (or legislative, if unorganized) approval, while the NRC retains licensing, construction, operation, safety and security authority.
regions.microreactor_activity: An Alaska Center for Energy and Power (ACEP)/Strategies 360 public-opinion survey, presented to the Alaska House Resources Committee on April 24, 2026, found awareness of advanced/microreactors rose from 'about a quarter' of respondents in 2023 to 'about 40%' in 2026, and that giving survey respondents 'a brief, neutral description of microreactors... increased measured support by about 10 percentage points.' No new nuclear-specific bill was found introduced in the 2025-2026 (34th) Legislature beyond SB 177's continuing regulatory implementation.
blockers: No 2026 legislative update found beyond SB 177 (2022) and its 2023 implementing regulation; the framework is settled but not further expanded
Public awareness of microreactors, while rising, was still only ~40% as of the April 2026 survey
regions.microreactor_read: Alaska's enabling law is the most settled of any region in this file: a siting statute and an implementing regulation have both been in force, unchanged, since August 2023, and public support is measurably rising. The gate on any Alaska deployment is now a utility's own commercial decision, not state law.

regions.power_system: Nukissiorfiit, Greenland's sole state-owned utility, supplies electricity, water and (in some places) heat to 'approximately 56,000 residents across 17 towns and 54 settlements' with 'no nationwide or regional electricity grid' -- every town and settlement is its own isolated system. Hydropower stations exist only at Nuuk, Sisimiut, Ilulissat and Tasiilaq; 'the power stations in all other towns and settlements are operated with diesel generators.' Nukissiorfiit reports about 72% of its energy from renewables (mostly hydro), targeting fossil-free supply by 2030.
regions.price: No DKK/kWh tariff sheet found (Nukissiorfiit's price pages 404'd); Nukissiorfiit states it subsidizes rates uniformly across Greenland to offset the gap between cheap hydro towns and small diesel-only settlements

regions.nuclear_position: Greenland's own Uranium Act (Greenland Parliament Act No. 20) 'came into force' on 2 December 2021 and bans 'prospecting, exploration, and exploitation of uranium' as well as any other mineral resource whose 'average uranium content' exceeds '100 ppm by weight.' On 26 June 2026 Greenland's government rejected Energy Transition Minerals' licence-renewal application for the Kvanefjeld/Kuannersuit deposit, stating 'further exploration in the area is not deemed likely to lead to the discovery of deposits that can be exploited in accordance with the Uranium Act.' Denmark, which controls defense and largely leaves mineral/energy policy to Greenland's home rule but retains the 1985 nationwide nuclear-power ban's legal legacy, announced in January 2026 that it is reviewing that 40-year ban: 'Denmark is considering building small modular nuclear reactors to meet its energy needs... which would bring an end to its 1985 ban on nuclear power,' after the Danish parliament 'agreed in early 2025 to begin examining new nuclear power technologies.' No specific Greenland carve-out or position within that Danish review was found.
regions.microreactor_activity: None found. The Danish SMR review is national and does not name Greenland; Nukissiorfiit has made no public statement on nuclear power.
blockers: The Uranium Act bans uranium mining/byproducts above 100 ppm, and Greenland's government has just (2026) shown it will enforce that against a major rare-earth project (Kvanefjeld)
Denmark's own nuclear review is at an early, information-gathering stage with no timeline for a political decision
No town or settlement publishes a load anywhere near even the smallest current microreactor design; the entire population (~56,000) is spread across 71 separate systems
regions.microreactor_read: Greenland is the least-prepared civilian buyer in this file: no enabling law, no utility study, and its parent state is only beginning to reconsider a 40-year nuclear ban. A reactor sale here depends on Denmark's still-open 2026 SMR review landing somewhere favorable, which has not yet happened.

regions.power_system: Yukon Energy runs a predominantly hydro grid (Whitehorse/Aishihik/Mayo) backstopped by LNG and diesel for winter peaking; low water in the Aishihik reservoir constrained winter 2025-26 output, and Yukon Energy is building a 15 MW thermal power centre in South Whitehorse using relocated rental diesel units. LNG plants held 13.2 MW (8.7%) of 2024 installed capacity per Yukon government statistics.

regions.nuclear_position: No territorial ban. On April 22, 2026, the Government of Yukon signed a formal partnership agreement with the Government of Ontario 'to strengthen collaboration on energy development, with a focus on improving long-term reliability and exploring emerging technologies such as small modular reactors.'
regions.microreactor_activity: Under the April 2026 Yukon-Ontario agreement, 'Ontario Power Generation and Yukon Energy will collaborate on the necessary groundwork to deploy SMRs to Yukon's grid,' covering 'nuclear energy, SMRs and microreactors including technological readiness, regulatory frameworks, supply chains, economics and financing, nuclear waste management and public and Indigenous engagement.' Yukon's energy minister, Ted Laking, framed it as a direct response to winter reliability: 'Our electricity grid is under strain and will soon be unable to meet the needs of the territory... we require significant investment in new generation capacity we can rely on in our coldest and darkest months of the year.' This is an assessment/knowledge-sharing agreement, not a project commitment, contract or site selection.
blockers: The agreement is explicitly exploratory ('help inform Yukon's assessment of whether SMRs could play a role'), with no project, site or vendor named
No Yukon-specific nuclear siting or licensing framework exists yet; the territory would rely on federal CNSC licensing and whatever regulatory groundwork the Ontario partnership produces
Yukon Energy's near-term capital is committed to the 15 MW South Whitehorse thermal centre and existing hydro assets
regions.microreactor_read: Yukon is the only Canadian territory with a named, dated, government-to-government nuclear partnership (April 2026) driven explicitly by a winter capacity shortfall; it is an assessment stage, but it is further along the policy path than Nunavut or NWT.

Canada's energy regulator puts NWT's 'estimated generating capacity' at 233 MW total, of which diesel plants 'accounted for 68%... in 2021.' The territorial utility, NTPC, operates diesel plants ranging from under 0.1 MW (Buffalo Junction) to 27.66 MW (a diesel combustion turbine at Yellowknife).

New this pass: the Kivalliq Hydro-Fibre Link (Nukik Corporation, Inuit-owned) proposes a 1,200 km, 150 MW transmission and fibre line from Manitoba's grid to five Kivalliq communities and at least one gold mine.

regions.nuclear_position: No territorial nuclear ban or enabling law found. QEC's own 2023-2026 Corporate Plan does not mention nuclear power (established in the 2026-09-02 pass). New: the federal Department of National Defence confirmed in August 2026 that it 'has launched a multi-year program to see whether a small nuclear reactor can be deployed in the Arctic,' funding the defence company Canadian Strategic Missions Corporation (CSMC) with $4.5 million in July 2026 'to advance Canadian-made energy solutions that will secure the North.'
regions.microreactor_activity: Kivalliq Hydro-Fibre Link schedule/funding, updated this pass: the Government of Canada's most recent dedicated funding announcement (March 2024) added $2.8 million to the project's development phase (on top of $11.6 million already provided for planning/feasibility), stating 'construction is expected to begin by 2028.' Since then, Nukik Corporation reports filing a Transmission Service Request with Manitoba Hydro (by December 2025) and becoming 'the first Arctic electricity developer in North America to be certified by the Midcontinent Independent System Operator (MISO)'; on July 7, 2026 the governments of Nunavut and Manitoba signed an MOU reaffirming 'Manitoba's commitment to provide 50 megawatts of firm electric capacity to the project.' No newer construction-start or financial-close date than 2028 was found. Separately, on the federal nuclear-for-the-North question: CSMC's CEO Daniel Sax said the company is 'working on building... very small nuclear reactors deployable into the Arctic to replace the diesel generators that are up there,' with 'a demonstration of the nuclear reactor by 2028 and then... this technology into the field by 2030,' and 'it's still unclear where in the North it will go.' Canadian Nuclear Laboratories' Ryan Clarke separately noted the North is 'already in an energy deficit.'
blockers: Kivalliq Hydro-Fibre Link construction is not expected to begin before 2028, and no financial close date was found
The federal microreactor-for-the-Arctic program is explicitly pre-siting: 'it's still unclear where in the North it will go,' with a 2028 demonstration and 2030 field target
Permafrost-melt risk from reactor waste heat and Arctic nuclear-waste storage were both raised as open questions by Canadian Nuclear Laboratories in the same August 2026 reporting
regions.microreactor_read: Nunavut now has two parallel federal tracks -- a 150 MW transmission alternative (Kivalliq, construction not before 2028) and a dedicated federal microreactor program (demonstration by 2028, field deployment by 2030) -- neither of which has picked a site; QEC's own interim rates ($555-1,130/MWh) remain the strongest economic case in this entire file for a reactor to beat.

regions.power_system: Nunatsiavut's five communities (Nain, Hopedale, Postville, Makkovik, Rigolet) are each an isolated diesel microgrid operated by Newfoundland and Labrador Hydro, unconnected to the provincial grid and resupplied by ship in the ice-free season; Nain's own generating station is listed at 3.86 MW (diesel genset, commissioned 1974). regions.power_system: Longyearbyen (Svalbard) closed the world's northernmost coal power plant on 19 October 2023 and switched to a temporary diesel plant while it builds toward an all-renewable supply; the coal-to-diesel transition itself was budgeted at 'NOK 212 million,' with the associated Mine 7 coal mine closing by summer 2025. In mainland northern Norway, Norsk Kjernekraft has signed cooperation/study agreements covering at least nine municipalities nationwide, including the northern municipalities of Narvik and Vardo; Narvik's municipal development company Futurum has formed 'Narvik Kjernekraft AS' with Norsk Kjernekraft to investigate SMR-based power plants. In Finland, Steady Energy (a VTT spinout) is marketing its LDR-50 reactor, rated at 'maximum heating power 50 MW per reactor module' for district heating, desalination and industrial steam, with letters of intent from the cities of Kuopio, Helsinki, Jyvaskyla (Alva) and, most recently, Kerava (Keravan Energia).

regions.nuclear_position: Norway has no nationwide nuclear-power ban and several municipalities (including the northern towns of Narvik and Vardo) have signed exploratory agreements with Norsk Kjernekraft. Finland permits nuclear power and already operates large reactors; Steady Energy's LDR-50 district-heat design is pursuing city-level letters of intent rather than a national policy change. Svalbard's own governance (the Norwegian state, via the Svalbard Treaty framework) has made no nuclear statement; its post-coal plan is diesel-then-renewables, not nuclear.
regions.microreactor_activity: Narvik: 'Narvik Kjernekraft AS' formed with Norsk Kjernekraft to begin 'planning a formal assessment phase' for possible SMR construction -- exploratory, no reactor size or in-service date set. Steady Energy: LDR-50 letters of intent signed with multiple Finnish cities, still at feasibility/permitting-scoping stage, with a company target of a first LDR-50 plant 'by 2030.' No microreactor activity found at Longyearbyen itself.
blockers: Longyearbyen's own plan is renewables by 2030, not nuclear; no SMR proposal was found for Svalbard specifically
Narvik/Vardo agreements are pre-feasibility ('investigate, and possibly plan, build and operate') with no site, size or schedule set
Steady Energy's LDR-50 has signed customer interest but no LDR-50 unit has yet been built anywhere
regions.microreactor_read: Northern Norway (Narvik, Vardo) and Finland's district-heat cities are the most advanced Nordic microreactor prospects in named-agreement terms, but all remain pre-feasibility; Svalbard itself, despite being the most extreme and best-known cold, remote, post-coal town in the region, has no reactor proposal at all.

regions.region: Polar research stations (Antarctica and Greenland ice sheet)
regions.jurisdiction: Antarctic Treaty System / Danish autonomous territory (research stations, not a national jurisdiction)
regions.power_system: The only civilian nuclear power precedent at either pole is the US Navy's PM-3A reactor at McMurdo Station, Antarctica: a 'pressurised-water reactor, with a capacity of 1.8 megawatts' by one account and '1,500 kilowatt' by another, which 'operated from March 1962 - September 1972' and displaced 'the need to deliver millions of gallons of fuel oil.' Today, US Antarctic and Greenland-ice-sheet stations (e.g. Summit Station, Greenland, run on behalf of the National Science Foundation at 3,200 m elevation) are diesel-generator powered, resupplied by aircraft (LC-130 airlift) given the absence of any road or port access.
regions.price: No $/gallon or $/MWh fuel-logistics figure was found for Summit Station or McMurdo

regions.nuclear_position: No nuclear ban specific to research stations; the Antarctic Treaty System restricts nuclear explosions and radioactive waste disposal in Antarctica but has historically permitted power reactors (PM-3A operated under it). No current proposal to re-introduce nuclear power at any US, Greenland or Antarctic research station was found.
regions.microreactor_activity: None found for any current station. PM-3A remains a one-off historical case, shut down for cause (a water leak judged 'impractical to repair,' compounded by the cost of its required 25-person crew and 'concerns over possible chloride stress corrosion').
blockers: PM-3A's own history is a cautionary precedent, not an endorsement: it was down more than a quarter of the time and required an expensive dedicated crew before being decommissioned
No current station operator (NSF, the US Antarctic Program) has an active nuclear proposal
Fuel-logistics cost data specific to any single station (e.g. Summit) is not published in a form this pass could locate or fetch
regions.microreactor_read: The historical McMurdo PM-3A case is the only civilian precedent for polar reactor power anywhere in this file, and it argues both ways: it proved a reactor can displace millions of gallons of resupply fuel, but its 1972 shutdown for a maintenance failure and its need for a 25-person crew are exactly the reliability and staffing risks a modern remote microreactor pitch has to answer.

cases.summary: Red Dog, Teck's zinc mine in Northwest Alaska on land partly owned by NANA Regional Corporation, is adding an 8.8 MW solar farm that Tugliq Energy, a Canadian independent power producer, will build and operate, selling power back to Teck under a PPA still being negotiated on price and terms. The mine draws about 25 MW and burns roughly 40,000 gallons of diesel a day; the solar addition is expected to supply about 2 MW during summer months, roughly 8% of demand. Separately, Teck reported in July 2026 that its Red Dog Mine Life Extension project (the Anarraaq and Aktigiruq zinc deposits, one of the world's largest undeveloped zinc resources) is progressing, with a connecting road substantially complete and C$200-250 million budgeted for 2026 engineering and drilling -- work that could extend the mine well past the existing Aqqaluk pit's ~2031 exhaustion date.
cases.microreactor_read: Red Dog is already building the deal shape a reactor vendor would need -- third-party-owned generation behind the fence, selling power back under a PPA -- at a mine whose life may now extend well past 2031; a reactor pitch here has to beat an undisclosed solar PPA price on a diesel base of roughly 40,000 gallons/day.

cases.name: Graphite One / Graphite Creek Project power plan
cases.capacity: 12.5 MW forecast draw per 2025 reporting (an earlier feasibility study cited 4 MW rising to 6 MW); default plan is a trio of diesel generators
cases.summary: Graphite One's Graphite Creek graphite mine on Alaska's Seward Peninsula, targeting first production around 2030, is forecast to draw 12.5 MW of power -- 'over twice the amount of power the entire city of Nome draws' -- against an earlier feasibility-study estimate of 4 MW rising to 6 MW after five years. The company's leading proposal remains a trio of diesel generators (one on standby), but its own SVP of Operations named nuclear power as a genuine option in April 2025 reporting, alongside wind (strong resource, long lead time) and solar (good in summer only), citing zero carbon footprint against two conditions: vendor maturity and social acceptability. No vendor, RFP or financing decision has been made for any option.
cases.microreactor_read: Graphite One is the clearest pre-construction Alaska mine naming nuclear power as an option, at a forecast load (12.5 MW) inside the 1-20 MW band; a vendor has a multi-year window before 2030 production to prove a design mature and accepted enough to displace the company's default diesel-genset plan.

cases.summary: The Kivalliq Hydro-Fibre Link is a proposed 1,200 km, 150 MW transmission and fibre line connecting Manitoba Hydro's grid to five Kivalliq, Nunavut communities (Arviat, Baker Lake, Chesterfield Inlet, Rankin Inlet, Whale Cove) and at least one gold mine, replacing diesel. As of this pass, the federal government has committed $2.8 million (2024, on top of $11.6 million for earlier planning) toward development-phase engineering and environmental work, with construction 'expected to begin by 2028'; developer Nukik Corporation has since filed a Transmission Service Request with Manitoba Hydro, become MISO-certified, and on 2026-07-07 secured a Nunavut-Manitoba government MOU committing Manitoba to supply 50 MW of firm capacity to the project.
cases.microreactor_read: This is the explicit non-nuclear alternative a reactor has to beat in Nunavut: a 150 MW grid-import project with a 2028 construction target and a firm 50 MW capacity commitment already signed, competing for the same diesel-displacement dollar as any Kivalliq microreactor pitch.

answers.question: Would NANA extend the land-and-PPA structure it gave TUGLIQ's solar project to a relocatable reactor, and what does 40,000 gallons a day come to per MWh at Teck's delivered price?
answers.finding: Neither original figure is newly disclosed: Teck has still not published a $/gallon or $/MWh diesel cost for Red Dog, and no NANA statement on an ownership stake or PPA-style structure for a reactor was found, both consistent with the 2026-09-02 pass. What is new this pass: Teck reported in July 2026 that its Red Dog Mine Life Extension project (the Anarraaq and Aktigiruq zinc deposits, 6-12 miles north of the current mill) is progressing, with a connecting road 'substantially completed' and C$200-250 million budgeted for the extension project in 2026. Aktigiruq alone hosts 42.2 million metric tons of indicated resource averaging 15.8% zinc, described as 'one of the world's largest undeveloped zinc resources.' This matters commercially because the mine's previously assumed 2031-2032 closure -- which any reactor's payback period depends on outliving -- may now be a conservative floor rather than a hard end date, though Teck has not itself given a revised closure year. The 8.8 MW Tugliq solar PPA remains under price negotiation as of March 2026 reporting and stays the operative precedent for how a reactor deal would likely be structured (third-party build-own-operate, selling power back under contract).
